case_study_insert.main_stem: Harbourlink City Breaks (HCB) is a partnership in the travel and tourism sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2015 by Elena Vasquez, the partnership designs short-break packages across European capital cities and uses a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership from the managing partner. HCB plans to invest $900,000 in launching a premium '48-hour signature city break' programme with exclusive hotel partnerships, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $300,000 of new partner capital. It has fixed costs of $3,050,000 a year, a variable cost of $1,240 a unit and a selling price of $1,850, and currently produces 10,800 units a year (one unit is one city-break package sold). HCB faces two problems: labour turnover among customer service staff has reached 29%, and seasonal operations absenteeism stands at 14% during the summer peak.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary (September 2026): HCB surveyed 900 recent customers; 67% prefer the planned '48-hour signature city break' concept, and the average booking value last year was $1,710. Booking satisfaction averaged 8.6 out of 10, and review scores average 4.6 out of 5 across 3,400 online reviews. Last-minute bookings (within 14 days of departure) now account for 31% of sales, and the cancellation rate is 4.2%. Online direct bookings grew 38% after a website relaunch, and average travel agent commission paid is 12%.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harbourlink City Breaks as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 6.0% to 6.75%, raising borrowing costs on variable-rate expansion loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $11.42 to $12.10 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills for customer service and operations staff. (3) Short-haul flight prices and hotel contracted rates have risen 9.4% year-on-year, while consumer spending on city breaks grew 5.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: HCB plans to finance part of its signature city break launch with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for HCB of using new partner capital instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: New partner capital of $300,000 carries no interest and no fixed repayment schedule, unlike the $600,000 bank loan at a time when the base interest rate has risen to 6.75%. That protects HCB's $3,050,000 fixed costs from an immediate lift in debt service, and preserves cash for the signature programme's launch marketing and contracted flight and hotel rates, which have already risen 9.4% year-on-year.

Point 2: Partner capital strengthens the partnership's unity and commitment: partners who invest more capital have a direct financial stake in the signature programme's success, reinforcing autocratic decision-making with aligned incentives and reducing pressure for short-term distributions. The bank loan stays unused or partially drawn, protecting HCB's credit line for later expansion phases, avoiding lender covenants on how the programme is marketed, and keeping ownership and control fully with Elena Vasquez and her fellow partners. The downside is scale: partner capital is finite, so if the signature programme outgrows plan, the partnership may still need the bank loan later — but it would then negotiate from a position of strength, with bookings of 10,800 units already proven and fixed costs unchanged.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Harbourlink City Breaks and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: HCB is launching its premium '48-hour signature city break' programme. Consider television advertising, targeted digital marketing (search and social ads), or print advertising in in-flight magazines. Which should HCB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television advertising: TV would give HCB national reach and prestige, positioning the premium programme as aspirational across the whole country. However, a 40-employee partnership financing $900,000 of launch costs cannot absorb seven-figure advertising bills, and TV wastes spend on audiences outside its European capital routes; the 31% last-minute booking pattern also rewards fast digital conversion rather than broad emotional build-up months in advance.

Targeted digital marketing: Search and social adverts reach exactly the 67% of surveyed customers who prefer the signature concept, captured while they actively research city breaks, and can retarget visitors who abandon bookings with the $1,710 average booking value in view. Costs are low, targeting is precise by geography, age and interest, results are measurable through the 38% direct-booking growth, and digital suits mobile-first last-minute buyers perfectly.

Print advertising in in-flight magazines: In-flight placements reach exactly the air-travel audience most likely to buy European city breaks, and the glossy format suits a premium programme with exclusive hotel partnerships. However, placement depends on airline deals, reach is tied to specific routes, and print lacks the immediacy, measurement and low cost-per-conversion of digital; it also cannot retarget a reader who has closed the magazine.

Recommendation: HCB should choose targeted digital marketing. It reaches the precise preference segment identified in its research, matches the 31% last-minute booking behaviour and 38% direct-booking shift, delivers measurable bookings per dollar, and fits a $900,000 launch budget. Television is rejected as untargeted and unaffordable for a 40-person partnership; in-flight print is rejected as route-limited and immeasurable, though HCB should add a small in-flight placement on its busiest route once the digital campaign proves conversion, and layer agent-commission incentives on top.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HCB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HCB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and in-flight print are rejected.

questions.question_text: HCB's labour turnover among customer service staff has reached 29% and seasonal operations absenteeism is 14%. Explain two benefits for HCB of using job enrichment for its customer service team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job enrichment — giving service agents ownership of whole bookings from enquiry to post-trip follow-up, plus discretion to resolve complaints up to an agreed limit — satisfies esteem and self-actualisation needs (Maslow) and replaces scripted, repetitive call-handling. Agents who own a case solve problems faster, reducing cancellations below the current 4.2% and complaints about delays, and feel too valued to resign — directly attacking the 29% labour turnover.

Point 2: Empowered agents handle the 31% of bookings made within 14 days of departure with far more confidence and judgment, upgrading confused callers to the $1,710 signature programme where appropriate. Fewer escalations free Elena Vasquez and the partners from autocratic day-to-day firefighting, improving the 8.6 out of 10 booking satisfaction and protecting the 4.6 review score that drives the 38% direct-booking growth — while self-managed autonomy also means less supervision needed when summer absenteeism hits 14%. Enriched agents also spot natural upsell moments for the signature programme — inclusive transfers, room upgrades, theatre add-ons — that a scripted call-handler would miss, lifting the $1,710 average booking value at zero extra marketing cost.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HCB's turnover, absenteeism and customer journey.

questions.question_text: HCB must decide how to sell the new signature city break programme. Consider selling mainly through independent travel agents (12% average commission) or selling mainly direct through HCB's own website. Which should HCB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Independent travel agents: Agents bring immediate high-street reach, trusted advice for premium packaged holidays and access to customers who prefer face-to-face consultation; the 12% average commission is a predictable cost of sale, and agents can explain the exclusive hotel partnerships persuasively. However, 12% commission on a $1,850 package is about $222 per booking (12% of $1,850 = $222) — at 10,800 units that is over $2.3 million a year (10,800 × $222 = $2,397,600) — and agents may steer clients to whichever package pays the richest commission rather than HCB's programme, diluting the premium positioning and margin.

Direct via HCB's own website: Direct sales capture the full margin, deepen customer data for remarketing, and match the 38% growth in direct bookings after the website relaunch plus the 31% last-minute segment that converts online. Costs are website maintenance and digital marketing rather than per-booking commission; the risk is losing older customers who still prefer agents, and carrying the full service burden without any agent advocacy.

Decision: HCB should choose selling mainly direct through its own website, with agents used selectively for premium and group bookings. Direct sales protect the $610 contribution ($1,850 − $1,240) per package and compound the online momentum already proven by the 38% direct-booking surge; mass agent reliance at 12% commission would transfer millions of margin to intermediaries and blur the premium brand. Pure agent distribution is rejected as too expensive and uncontrollable; a blended approach retains agents only where they add value above 12% of contribution, such as incentive-travel corporate accounts. Elena Vasquez should also cap agent allocation to a minority of signature-programme inventory, reviewed quarterly against direct margin, so the partnership never becomes dependent on intermediaries to fill its flagship departures.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two distribution options with limited application to HCB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both distribution options in the context of HCB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of HCB with a well-justified decision covering margin, channel economics and brand control.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HCB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $3,050,000 ÷ ($1,850 − $1,240) = $3,050,000 ÷ $610 = 5,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 5,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $1,850 − $1,240 = $610. Answer: contribution per unit is $610.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HCB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. HCB can compare the 5,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 10,800 packages, a margin of safety of 5,800 units, confirming the partnership trades well above break-even and can absorb a $600,000 bank loan without distress even if signature-programme demand starts slowly.
2. With $610 contribution ($1,850 − $1,240) per package, management can model commission structures: at 12% commission (about $222 per package, since 12% of $1,850 = $222), agent-sold packages still out-earn their variable cost, informing whether HCB pays $222 to agents or keeps the full $610 per package by selling direct.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $3,050,000 and $610 contribution helps HCB set the minimum group size and price the exclusive hotel partnerships in the $900,000 signature programme so that each package covers its variable cost and helps recover fixed costs.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($3,050,000 ÷ 10,800 units + $1,240 = $1,522.41 a unit) to track margin per departure week, identify which capitals' contracted rates drifted above the 9.4% average increase, and decide whether to renegotiate hotel terms or raise the signature selling price above $1,850.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 5,000 units a year, computed as $3,050,000 fixed costs divided by $610 contribution per package (selling price $1,850 less variable cost $1,240). At the current 10,800 packages, HCB operates a margin of safety of 5,800 units, confirming the partnership can service the $600,000 bank loan while the signature programme launches. (ii) Contribution per unit = $610 per city-break package sold, the amount every package adds toward fixed costs and partner drawings. (iii) Four applied uses: first, tracking the margin of safety against any demand softening if variable-rate borrowing costs bite at 6.75%; second, modelling agent economics, where 12% commission of about $222 per package must stay below one-third of contribution for agent-sold packages to out-earn break-even; third, pricing the $900,000 signature programme and setting minimum group sizes for the exclusive hotel partnerships; fourth, unit-cost benchmarking at $1,522.41 per package ($3,050,000 ÷ 10,800 + $1,240) to manage contracted-rate drift across the capitals amid the 9.4% flight and hotel rate rise. Together these uses let Elena Vasquez test launch pricing, channel mix and contract renegotiations against the break-even line each month.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HCB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HCB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.58 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.36 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.42 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.21 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $80,000 inventories + $520,000 trade receivables + $160,000 cash = $760,000; 2025 current assets = $95,000 + $610,000 + $140,000 = $845,000. Current liabilities rose from $480,000 to $620,000. 2024: $760,000 ÷ $480,000 = 1.58; 2025: $845,000 ÷ $620,000 = 1.36. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($760,000 − $80,000) ÷ $480,000 = $680,000 ÷ $480,000 = 1.42; 2025 = ($845,000 − $95,000) ÷ $620,000 = $750,000 ÷ $620,000 = 1.21.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened on both measures. Current liabilities jumped 29% from $480,000 to $620,000 while cash fell from $160,000 to $140,000, so HCB now covers short-term debts less comfortably than a year ago. Trade receivables rose from $520,000 to $610,000 — agents and corporate clients are paying slowly, tying up cash that HCB needs for supplier payments to airlines and hotels contracted at rates up 9.4%. The stricter measure slipped from 1.42 to 1.21, still above 1.0, but the direction is wrong precisely when HCB is about to draw a $600,000 bank loan and a $900,000 signature-programme investment. Rising inventories of $95,000 are also working-capital strain, not strength, for an asset-light tour operator that should hold almost no stock.

Conclusion: HCB's financial position has NOT improved. Both measures declined, cash fell, and the slip is driven by ballooning trade receivables and current liabilities rather than by any investment that pays back quickly. HCB should tighten agent credit terms, collect deposits on signature bookings, convert agent-sold holidays to shorter credit cycles, and avoid drawing the bank loan until receivables fall materially below $610,000.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether HCB's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HCB of launching the premium '48-hour signature city break' programme.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The signature programme targets the 67% of surveyed customers who prefer the concept and carries higher spend than the current $1,710 average booking value, lifting revenue per unit and HCB's $610 contribution ($1,850 − $1,240) while these premium customers show greater loyalty to exclusive hotel partnerships. It differentiates HCB from generic online travel agents, justifies investment of $900,000 with partner capital and a bank loan, and matches the 5.6% growth in consumer city-break spending.

Disadvantage: The programme concentrates HCB's risk in a small number of exclusive hotel partnerships — if one capital's contracted rates fail or a hotel underdelivers, the premium brand promise collapses publicly via the 4.6 review score. Setup costs of $900,000 consume the partnership's flexibility, the $600,000 bank loan adds fixed interest at a 6.75% base rate, and any execution failure (late transfers, overbooked rooms) would hit the already-strained 29% labour turnover in customer service, multiplying complaints precisely when HCB needs flawless delivery to convert the 67% interested segment into paying customers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HCB's research, costs and launch.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.75%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase to $12.10 and the 9.4% rise in short-haul flight prices and hotel contracted rates will affect HCB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (6.0% to 6.75%): On HCB's $600,000 variable-rate bank loan, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $4,500 a year in interest ($600,000 × 0.75% = $4,500), lifting fixed costs above $3,050,000. Higher rates may also cool discretionary city-break demand at the margin, and could raise the cost of drawing the $900,000 signature-programme funding. The direct impact is the smallest of the three, is fully computable from insert figures, can be capped by fixing the loan rate, and does not erode the $610 contribution ($1,850 − $1,240) per package.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $12.10 per hour from April 2026): Appendix 3 gives both rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.68 ($12.10 − $11.42 = $0.68). The annual cost cannot be computed from the insert because the number of minimum-wage hours is not stated; what can be shown is the threshold at which this factor exceeds the interest rise — it does so once HCB pays more than roughly 6,618 minimum-wage hours a year ($4,500 ÷ $0.68 ≈ 6,618), a level comfortably exceeded by a 40-employee operator with customer service, operations and support staff. This lands on a team already carrying 29% labour turnover and 14% summer absenteeism, so the award must be matched with engagement, flexible rostering and Herzberg-style responsibility if it is not to widen churn alongside cost.

Short-haul flight prices and hotel contracted rates (up 9.4% year-on-year): Appendix 3 names the two largest cost components of almost any short-haul city-break package — airfares and hotels. No share of the $1,240 variable cost is stated, so no legitimate total exists in the insert; anything precise would be invented. What can be shown is an upper bound built only on insert figures: applying the full 9.4% to the entire $1,240 gives at most about $116.56 per package ($1,240 × 9.4% = $116.56), i.e. roughly $1,258,848 a year across the current 10,800 packages as an absolute ceiling — real exposure will be lower but can only be lower by the fare/hotel share, which the insert does not disclose. What is certain is that flight and hotel costs scale with every unit sold, that they are contracted wholesale rather than discretionary, and that HCB cannot refinance them — it must renegotiate, re-time or re-route them before the $900,000 signature launch hard-wires new exclusivity clauses.

Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in short-haul flight prices and hotel contracted rates will have the greatest impact. It attaches to the two largest structural components of every one of the 10,800 packages sold, sits inside the $1,240 variable cost, exceeds the wage floor's per-hour exposure of $0.68 on typical annual totals by a clear margin in any plausible reading, and dwarfs the exactly computable $4,500 interest rise. The 6.0% minimum wage increase to $12.10 is second — real, unavoidable, and risky given 29% turnover and 14% absenteeism — while the 0.75 point interest rise is the smallest and can be fixed away. HCB must renegotiate contracted rates now, shift marketing to the direct channel (online direct bookings grew 38% after the website relaunch) to keep the full $610 contribution, time departures around fare cycles, and reserve any signature-price rises for the 67% of surveyed customers who prefer the concept, protecting contribution while the $900,000 programme proves itself.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HCB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HCB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HCB with a well-justified judgement that flight and hotel input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
